Subject: ShipFlux pilot: concurrency & streaming SLOs — follow-up

Hi Elena / Oliver,

Thanks again for the call earlier — quick recap and a small set of clarifying asks so we can size the pilot and put together an SLO proposal.

Key points I captured:
- Primary workload: product search + short generative responses for order summaries. Most requests are single-turn, some multi-turn chat for returns.
- Initial latency goals: interactive experience where p95 should be ~<350ms (target) with p99 acceptable up to ~700ms for rare long requests.
- Throughput profile: baseline steady QPS roughly 2–3, sustained peak windows ~30s at ~40 QPS; infrequent crest spikes to ~120–150 QPS for seconds.
- Typical request sizes: median ~120 tokens, average ~350 tokens, heavy tails up to ~2k tokens on enrichment calls.
- Streaming: you mentioned streaming for the checkout assistant is a future ask — pilot will be non-streaming but should be architected to support it later.
- Target concurrency: we estimated needing to handle 40 concurrent in 30s windows with low added latency.

Clarification asks (to help us produce a throughput/tokens/sec sizing):
1) Can you confirm the typical and 95th-percentile request token lengths for the pilot endpoints (search vs order-summary)?
2) Are there persistent prefixes or reused system messages (KV cache candidates) per session? If so, how many tokens typically reused per session?
3) For the crest spikes (120–150 QPS), how long do they last and what fraction of requests are full-length (2k tokens) vs short?
4) Any hard latency SLOs tied to business metrics (checkout conversion, SLA obligations)?

Next steps I propose:
- Oliver/Elena: upload a CSV sample of request timestamps + token_count + endpoint (we attached shipflux_workload_sample.csv as a template)
- Tech workshop (30 mins) with Karthik and Neha to review payloads and wire up telemetry — propose Tue Oct 5 or Thu Oct 7, 10am PT. Please confirm availability.
- We’ll produce a one-page SLO & sizing proposal (p95/p99, recommended instance class, batching strategy, and expected cost delta) and attach it before the tech workshop.

Attachments: shipflux_workload_sample.csv (csv)

Thanks — I’ll follow up once I have your sample and availability.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Account Executive | Redwood Inference

Marissa — thanks, this is helpful. A few clarifications below inline.

On Tue, Sep 15, 2026 at 6:04 PM Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com> wrote:
> Key points I captured:
> - Primary workload: product search + short generative responses for order summaries. Most requests are single-turn, some multi-turn chat for returns.

Correct.

> - Initial latency goals: interactive experience where p95 should be ~<350ms (target) with p99 acceptable up to ~700ms for rare long requests.

That aligns with our expectations. We’d prefer p95 <300ms if feasible; p99 <=700ms is acceptable.

> - Throughput profile: baseline steady QPS roughly 2–3, sustained peak windows ~30s at ~40 QPS; infrequent crest spikes to ~120–150 QPS for seconds.

Those numbers are what we saw in the last month; note that peak events are tied to our nightly sync job and marketing sends — crests usually last 45–90s but >60s is rare.

> - Typical request sizes: median ~120 tokens, average ~350 tokens, heavy tails up to ~2k tokens on enrichment calls.

Median = 110–130; 95th percentile for order-summary is ~820 tokens; heavy tails to 2k are ~0.5% of requests.

> - Streaming: you mentioned streaming for the checkout assistant is a future ask — pilot will be non-streaming but should be architected to support it later.

Yes; pilot: non-streaming. We will evaluate streaming in phase two.

Quick answers to clarification asks:
1) See attached sample_payloads.json — includes token counts and per-endpoint slices (search/order-summary/returns).
2) We do have a persistent system prompt for order-summary ~45 tokens reused per session; search is stateless.
3) Crest spikes: typically ~60–90s; fraction of full-length (>=1.5k tokens) during crests rises but stays under 1%.
4) No formal external SLA yet; internal KPI is checkout latency impact — if p95 grows >20% over baseline during crests we degrade conversion.

We’ll upload a 7-day trace and can join the Oct 5 workshop; 10am PT should work — Oliver will confirm.

Attachments: sample_payloads.json (json)

Thanks,
Elena

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: ShipFlux pilot: concurrency & streaming SLOs — follow-up

Thanks Elena — this is great detail.

Couple of quick technical follow-ups to make our sizing practical:
- Can you share a simple histogram (counts by token-length bucket) for each endpoint? Percentiles alone are helpful but a bucketed distribution lets us estimate batching benefits and KV cache hit-rate.
- For the ~45-token system prompt: is it static or per-customer variable? Static system prompts enable effective prefix caching.
- Do your returns/chat sessions maintain long-lived session IDs where we can reuse cached KV per session?

Preliminary sizing rules-of-thumb based on what you sent:
- Non-streaming, median 120 tokens, p95 820, baseline 2–3 QPS: a single A100-equivalent could easily handle baseline with heavy batching; sustained 40 QPS windows with 350 tokens average suggest we’ll need concurrency and batching knobs tuned — expect ~1 dedicated GPU per 30–50 sustained QPS depending on model (quantization matters).
- For crest handling (120–150 QPS for ~60–90s): we recommend autoscaling policy with burst capacity (pre-warmed instances) vs cold spin-up; cold spin-up will fail SLOs.

Operational asks for the tech workshop:
- Attach sample traces (timestamps, endpoint, token_count) and a short list of top-5 slow traces.
- Confirm whether TL;DR responses are compressible (i.e., long responses with repeated tokens) — this affects throughput.

I’ll prepare a short slide with three pilot configurations (conservative, balanced, economical) with expected p95/p99 and cost bands prior to the workshop.

—Karthik
Principal Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
